messages.subject: Questions about causal indicator models
messages.body_plain:
Hi,

I have a couple of questions related to causal indicator models. Consider the following example:

library(lavaan)

model <- "L1 =~ y1 + y2 + y3
L2 <~ 1*x1 + x2 + x3
L3 =~ y4 + y5 + y6
L3 ~ L2 + L1"

data.cov <- matrix(.5,9,9)
diag(data.cov) <- 1
colnames(data.cov) <- rownames(data.cov) <- c(paste("x",1:3,sep=""),paste("y",1:6,sep=""))
fit <- sem(model, sample.cov = data.cov, sample.nobs = 100, fixed.x = TRUE)

inspect(fit)

There are two things that I do not get:

1) Why is the covariance between L1 and error term of L2 free in the psi matrix, but the variance of the error term of L2 is constrained to be zero? To me it would seem that constraining variance to be zero would logically imply that covariances are zero as well.

2) Why are all covariances between exogenous latent variable L1 and exogenous observed variables x1, x2, and x3 constrained to be zero?

Mikko

messages.body_plain:
It may be that the larger model is misspecified.  If there is a missing path (say, from #1 to #4 or from #2 to #4), then the path from #2 to #4 may be biased to compensate, producing a lower R2 for #3 when #4 is present.  If you add direct paths from #1 and #2 to #4, I bet you will see the decline in #3’s R2 disappear.

--Ed Rigdon

model1.syntax <- 'y ~ 1 * x1 + b2 * x2 + b3 * x3 + 0'

Alex

That is absolutely the problem.  This model is not identified because all possible residual correlations for all "calmness" indicators are freely estimated, rendering the common factor completely superfluous.  If you suspect many small residual correlations, you probably want to look into using a Bayesian approach with informative priors (an option not yet available using lavaan) -- see the 2012 paper on this web page for details, and the other links on that page provide applied examples:

Terry

Duncan--
     A structural model like this will be not identified without special conditions.  An econometrician using the rank and order conditions would want each of the two reciprocal dependents to have at least one other predictor that is not common to both reciprocal dependents, but it is possible to estimate this model as long as at least one of the two has an unshared predictor.  So a model like:
A ~ B
B ~ A
is not identified.
An econometrician would expect at least
A ~ B + C
B ~ A + D
C ~~ D   # probably
At a minimum, you would need:
A ~ B + C
B ~ A
and you might need to help that toward convergence by providing starting values.

Rigdon, Edward E. (1995), "A Necessary and Sufficient Identification Rule for Structural Models Estimated in Practice."  Multivariate Behavioral Research 30 (4), 359-84.

--Ed Rigdon

Mike--

messages.subject: Re: Bias in Weighted Least Squares Estimates
messages.subject_clean: Bias in Weighted Least Squares Estimates
messages.body_plain:
If the discrepancy does not go to zero with larger sample sizes, it
means that the model is misspecified. This is the foundation of
econometrics' Hausman test. ULS and DWLS only make assumptions
regarding the second order moments of the data, which you provide via
polychoric/polyserial correlations (and these may be misspecified in
their own right if the underlying data are not multivariate normal,
although you did simulate them as normal, so that should not be the
issue). In a continuous case with Pearson moment correlation not
having any of the weird problems, you can say that they estimate
parameters $\theta$ in $\sigma_{ij}=\sigma_{ij}(\theta)$ with only the
model structure being used to drive the estimates. Full WLS/ADF tries
to bring some assumptions about the fourth order moments of the data
(warranted if these assumptions are reasonably close to be true) via
correlations of $\sigma_{ij}$. The second moment of second moments are
obviously the fourth moments. If these assumptions are not warranted,
the estimates get fragile. The full WLS/ADF estimates are dealing with
$\sigma_{ij}=\sigma_{ij}(\theta)$ AND fourth order moment = function
of $\theta$, which has a different solution in population (unless you
have the fourth order moments matching those of the multivariate
normal, or probably the more general Satorra's asymptotic robustness
conditions), so the WLS estimates must be converging to that different
target.

Economists utilize Hausman tests to check whether their model
assumptions are satisfied by fitting a model with a robust method
(DWLS) and a method that is efficient when the model is perfect
(WLS/ADF/normal theory MLE). When the model assumptions are satisfied,
the difference is only due to the lesser efficiency of the former
method, so the difference between the estimates should be within
sampling variation. In case of WLS/ADF vs DWLS and ULS, though, it
seems to be hard to tell if the resulting difference between estimate
is a test on model *structure* (which is what most practitioners would
be interested in), or rather a test on *distribution* (non-normality
of the population) which is an inalienable assumption of the
WLS/ADF/NTMLE; it may well be the latter.

That you reproduced the problem in different packages is great, but I
would still hope to see less of a discrepancy between them. Otherwise,
the world of SEM cannot talk about DWLS as a *method*, only as a black
box churning the numbers. The Mx black box may be 2" x 5" x 3", and
lavaan's black box may be 3" x 7" x 1", and Mplus may be 4" x 3" x
undisclosed (you need to pay the license charge to figure out what
that last dimension is), and if all these black boxes produce
different numbers, I personally don't see any reason to trust any of
these numbers until I see an explanation put forth by a developer as
to why these numbers would differ.

-- Stas Kolenikov, PhD, PStat (ASA, SSC)

Statistical Association

messages.body_plain:
Fernando--
     Things to think about--
     1.  Think about how the factor scores reported by lavaan are computed.  The determinate part of a factor score is a prediction of the common factor based on all of the observed variables in the model--not just the ones that load on the factor.  Using the regression method for estimating this number, the formula is similar to that for regression weights--covariances divided by the inverse of the covariance matrix of the predictors (here, all observed variables).  You use all the same observed variables, and they are all still correlated with the factor, so there is much that is similar statistically
     2.  You say that the MIMIC model provides better fit, which I assume means a better chi-square value and derivatives.  But the chi-square value just tells you that there is more information in the data than is accounted for by your model.  That "more" may have nothing to do with this common factor, so it has no effect on the determinate part of the factor scores.
     3.  Remember that this is only the determinate part of the score.  There is also an indeterminate part.  This part could be very different across models.  The fewer indicators loading on the factor, the greater the indeterminacy--though using fewer indicators may lead to stronger loadings, which will offset that effect.
--Ed Rigdon

Guttman, L. (1955). The determinacy of factor score matrices with implications for five other basic problems of common-factor theory. The British Journal of Statistical Psychology, 8, 65-81.

Schönemann, P.H., & Steiger, J.H. (1976). Regression component analysis. British Journal of Mathematical and Statistical Psychology, 29, 175-189.

messages.body_plain:
I don't see what would stop you from running this model.  Does the syntax not work?  (make sure the variable names are consistent: Marriage vs. mariage).

A "Panel model" is fit to longitudinal data.  I don't see anything in your syntax that indicates you have measured the same variables repeatedly, but if that is what you have, you can just regress the first-occasion outcomes on your distal predictors, then regression second-occasion outcomes on the first-occasion outcomes, third-occasion outcomes on second-occasion outcomes, and so on. messages.body_plain:
Hi,

The HTMT index is calculated from the data covariance matrix and does not require a model to be estimated. It does basically the same thing as the AVE criterion. Both these essentially asses whether the factors are perfectly correlated, but that is not what the original idea of discriminant validity of measures is about. There is no evidence that I would be aware of that would show that either of these approaches would generally detect crossloading indicators.

You can calculate the HTML with the following code:

# Mean within- and between-block correlations
meanBlockCor <- (t(reflective) %*% (S*lower.tri(S)) %*% reflective) /
(t(reflective) %*% lower.tri(S) %*% reflective)
# Choose the blocks that have at least two reflective indicators
i <- which(colSums(reflective) > 1)
meanBlockCor <- meanBlockCor[i,i]
# Calculate the indices
htmt <- meanBlockCor*lower.tri(meanBlockCor) /
sqrt(diag(meanBlockCor) %o% diag(meanBlockCor))

Where S is the sample correlation matrix and reflective is a binary matrix indicating the factor loading matrix.

The chi square statistic will tell you if the model fits the data and if it does not, then you need to diagnose why that is the case.

Mikko

messages.body_plain:
Hi

AVE is the mean of squared standardized factor loadings. Here is an example how to calculate AVEs:

# load the lavaan package (only needed once per session)
library(lavaan)

# specify the model
HS.model <- ' visual  =~ x1 + x2 + x3
textual =~ x4 + x5 + x6
speed   =~ x7 + x8 + x9 '

# fit the model
fit <- cfa(HS.model, data=HolzingerSwineford1939)

# Extract the standardized loading matrix
loadMatrix <- inspect(fit, "std")$lambda

# Clear the zero loadings
loadMatrix[loadMatrix==0] <- NA

# Calculate mean squared loadings (i.e. AVEs)
apply(loadMatrix^2,2,mean, na.rm = TRUE)

Mikko

> Is it possible to assign a reliability coefficient to each indicator?

Assuming the unreliable part of each indicator is uncorrelated with the unreliable part of the other 4, the latent factor already represents the common variance among all 5 indicators, and their residual variances represent the unique variances of each indicator (which is a mix of reliable indicator-specific variance and unreliable error variance).  Assigning the complement of a reliability coefficient as the fixed error variance of an indicator is typically done only when you have a single-indicator factor, in which case you can't extract "common" variance among (nonexistent) multiple indicators.

Terry

I assume that because you are using product indicators (which are not normally distributed, and are typically highly kurtotic when made from centered variables), that you are using a robust estimator (MLR). If the difference test comes out negative, you can use a different formulation that was proposed to prevent this:

Hi, Rania

You should test for metric ans scalar invariance (I never recommend strict). A couple of reasons I would say, first is in fact there are not invariant problems due to the source of the data them the model will just pass the tests and you will be able to do latent parameter comparisons (means, variances), is a testable hypothesis, always better to test for it instead of assuming it. Second, the description that you gave is kind of an interpretation, technically, the factor loading invariance tests the structure of the shared variance between indicators, I dont think that the items came from websites etc is related to the correlation between items. The intercept invariance looks into intercept shifts, also I dont see it related to the source of the data.

In summary, my point of view would be that the source of the data is not necessary related to its behavior, and you can always test these hypothesis
